did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalmist describes his distress through the image of waters reaching his soul—a picture of profound danger and having no way out.

Did you know? The intensity of the persecution is compared to the number of hairs on his head, and his enemies are also called “enemies without cause.” The psalmist emphasizes that he must restore what he did not steal.

Did you know? Alongside his description of persecution, the psalmist acknowledges that God knows his folly and that his guilt is not hidden from Him. Thus, the chapter combines a complaint about injustice with self-examination.

Did you know? The psalmist is not asking only for personal deliverance; he fears that his disgrace will bring shame upon those who hope in the LORD and seek Him, and he asks that they not be put to shame because of him.
Did you know? The psalmist’s zeal for God’s house is portrayed as a force consuming him, and he describes the insults hurled at God as though they had fallen upon him.
Did you know? Wearing sackcloth serves in this chapter as a public expression of mourning and distress, but it also makes the psalmist an object of ridicule and mockery to those around him.

Did you know? After a series of descriptions of drowning, disgrace, and persecution, the psalmist defines his prayer as an appeal to the LORD in an “acceptable time” and asks for an answer through the power of His steadfast love and salvation.
Did you know? The chapter describes especially cruel treatment: instead of food, the psalmist is given gall, and instead of a drink for his thirst, vinegar.

Did you know? The psalmist declares that praise and thanksgiving to the LORD are more pleasing than a bull, described as having horns and split hooves. This verse thus emphasizes the value of gratitude.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, praise expands from humanity to all creation: the heavens, the earth, the seas, and everything that moves in them are called to praise God, alongside the promise of salvation for Zion and the rebuilding of Judah’s cities.
